passages.happening:
‘Shortly before the LORD took Elijah up to heaven in a whirlwind, Elijah and Elisha were on their way from Gilgal’ (verse 1). Three times Elijah asks Elisha to stay behind, first for Bethel, then for Jericho, then for the Jordan. Three times Elisha answers, “As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you” (verse 2). At Bethel and at Jericho the sons of the prophets ask Elisha whether he knows that the LORD will take his master away today. “Yes, I know,” he says. “Do not speak of it” (verse 3).

Fifty of the prophets stand at a distance as the two men reach the Jordan. Elijah rolls up his cloak and strikes the water, it parts, and they cross on dry ground (verse 8). Elijah asks what he can do for him before he is taken. “Please, let me inherit a double portion of your spirit,” Elisha replies (verse 9). It is a hard thing, Elijah says, but if Elisha sees him taken, it will be his (verse 10).

‘As they were walking along and talking together, suddenly a chariot of fire with horses of fire appeared and separated the two of them, and Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind’ (verse 11). Elisha cries out, “My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!” (verse 12). He sees Elijah no more, and he tears his clothes in two.
passages.hearers:
This chapter is the hinge between the Elijah stories at the end of 1 Kings and the Elisha stories that fill most of 2 Kings to chapter 13. At Horeb Elijah had been told to anoint Elisha to succeed him, and Elisha left his oxen to follow him. Now the handover is completed, about 852 BC. The question the chapter answers matters for the whole book: will the word of the LORD go on in Israel once its great prophet is gone?

The sons of the prophets were communities gathered around a leader, found at Bethel, Jericho and Gilgal in these chapters. The Gilgal here is probably a town in the hill country north of Bethel, since the two men go down from it to Bethel. The road ends across the Jordan, near where Moses died and where Israel had first crossed into the land.

A double portion was the share of the firstborn son, twice what each of his brothers received. Elisha is not asking to be twice as great as Elijah. He is asking to be his heir. His cry to Elijah as father fits that request, since a prophet's disciples could call their master father. The word for spirit, ruach, can mean wind, breath or the Spirit of the LORD, which suits a chapter where a storm takes one prophet and the Spirit rests on another.

The threefold pattern slows the story and builds suspense. The narrator never describes the whirlwind itself in detail. Elisha's cry and his torn clothes carry the moment.
passages.later: Of Enoch, Genesis says, ‘Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away’ (Genesis 5:24). The law gave the firstborn ‘a double portion of all that he has’ (Deuteronomy 21:17). And on the mountain with Jesus, ‘Elijah and Moses appeared before them, talking with Jesus’ (Mark 9:4).
passages.asks: Three times Elisha refused to stay behind. Ask what it would mean for you to keep close to what God is doing when others tell you to stay where you are. And ask whom you call father or mother in the faith, and what you hope to receive from them.

passages.t: Elijah's cloak, and a spring healed
passages.happening:
Elisha picks up the cloak that fell from Elijah and stands on the bank of the Jordan. He strikes the water and asks, “Where now is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” (verse 14). The water parts, and he crosses. The sons of the prophets from Jericho see it and say, “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha” (verse 15), and they bow before him.

They want to send fifty men to search for Elijah, in case the Spirit of the LORD has set him down on a mountain or in a valley. Elisha says no, then gives way when they press him. They search for three days and find nothing (verses 16-18).

At Jericho the men of the city tell him the place is good but ‘the water is bad and the land is unfruitful’ (verse 19). He asks for a new bowl with salt in it, throws the salt into the spring and says in the LORD's name, ‘I have healed this water. No longer will it cause death or unfruitfulness’ (verse 21). The water has been wholesome ‘to this day, according to the word spoken by Elisha’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The cloak, in Hebrew adderet, was the outer garment that marked Elijah as a prophet. He had thrown it over Elisha when he first called him, and now Elisha picks it up for good. The crossing of the Jordan frames the whole scene. Elijah strikes the water and crosses, then Elisha strikes it with the same cloak and crosses back, as Israel had once crossed under Joshua. The same power that parted the water for Elijah parts it for Elisha. Elisha's question is not about the cloak. It is about the LORD.

The search shows that the prophets did not yet understand what they had seen.

Jericho had been rebuilt in Ahab's day, at the cost of its builder's sons, under the curse Joshua had pronounced. Now the LORD heals its water. Salt was linked with purity and with covenant in Israel, and a new bowl, never used for anything common, suits a sacred act. The verb heal, rapha, is the one in the LORD's word to Israel after bitter water was made sweet at Marah. A copious spring beside the ancient mound at Tell es-Sultan, which tradition calls Elisha's spring, still waters the oasis.
passages.later: After the bitter water was made sweet at Marah, the LORD told Israel, ‘For I am the LORD who heals you’ (Exodus 15:26).
passages.asks: Elisha struck the water and asked where the God of Elijah was. Ask whether you trust the LORD himself, or only the people and things through which you have seen him work. And ask what bitter water in your town or your life you have stopped expecting God to heal.

passages.happening: Elisha goes up from Jericho to Bethel. As he walks up the road, ‘a group of boys came out of the city and jeered at him’ (verse 23). They chant, “Go up, you baldhead! Go up, you baldhead!” (verse 23). He turns, looks at them, and ‘called down a curse on them in the name of the LORD’ (verse 24). Two female bears come out of the woods and maul forty-two of them (verse 24). Elisha goes on to Mount Carmel and then back to Samaria (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Bethel was the royal shrine of the northern kingdom, where Jeroboam had set up one of the golden calves. That helps explain the hostility Elisha meets there.

The Hebrew words behind boys cover a wide range, from small children to young men, and the size of the crowd matters for understanding the scene. Their taunt, go up, may mock the report that Elijah had gone up, telling the new prophet to disappear as his master had. Shaving the head could mark mourning or a vow, and baldness was open to mockery. Whether Elisha was naturally bald or had shaved his head is not said.

The chapter sets two short signs of Elisha's authority side by side. At Jericho a word brings healing and life. At Bethel a word brings judgment.
passages.later: Among the covenant's warnings to a rebellious people, the law said, ‘I will send wild animals against you’ (Leviticus 26:22). When two disciples wanted to call down fire on a village that turned Jesus away, ‘Jesus turned and rebuked them’ (Luke 9:55).
passages.hard:
How could a prophet of God curse a crowd of youths, and have forty-two of them mauled by bears?

This is one of the most troubling scenes in the Bible, and it deserves honest attention. Several things in the text bear on it. The Hebrew words for the youths can mean young men as well as children, and a crowd of at least forty-two suggests a mob rather than a few small children. They came out of Bethel, the center of the calf worship that the prophets opposed, and their taunt may mock Elijah's going up. On this reading the scene is a public rejection of the LORD's prophet at the moment his work begins, and the judgment echoes the covenant warning of wild animals sent among a rebellious people.

Other interpreters accept all of this and still find the punishment severe, and they note that the narrator reports it without comment. The text does not say that the youths were killed, only that they were mauled. It presents the event as the LORD's judgment, not Elisha's personal revenge, since the curse is spoken in the LORD's name, and readers differ on how much that eases the difficulty. These notes do not settle it.

What can be said plainly is this. The scene gives no one today a warrant to harm anyone, to curse anyone who mocks them, or to wish harm on a child or a young person. When two of his disciples wanted to bring down judgment on people who rejected him, Jesus rebuked them. Anyone who carries God's word today carries it under that rebuke.
passages.asks: In a few verses the same prophet brings healing at Jericho and judgment at Bethel. Ask what it costs to mock what is holy. And ask how you answer people who mock your faith, and whether your answer looks more like the curse at Bethel or the rebuke Jesus gave his disciples.
